turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, thank you. Um, well, the main reason I’m here is that work has just become... it's become incredibly overwhelming lately. I'm a registered nurse, and I work on a really busy floor, which I usually love, you know? I went to grad school for this, I know my clinical stuff, but recently—or I guess for a while now, if I'm being honest—I just lose my train of thought constantly. Like, constantly. It’s actually getting to the point where I’m terrified I’m going to fall behind or drop the ball on something important. 

For example, I'll be at the nurse's station trying to figure out a patient flow issue—trying to coordinate who is discharging so we can get the next admission up from the ER, which is a whole complicated puzzle in itself—and then an IV pump will start beeping three rooms down. Not even my patient's pump, just *a* pump. Or someone will ask another nurse a random question, or a call light goes off at the end of the hall, and it's like... my brain just completely resets. I get pulled away by the noise, and suddenly I’m standing there and I have absolutely forgotten what patient flow issue I was working on. I just stare at the screen having no idea what I was doing three seconds ago. And then I have to start my whole thought process all over again, and it’s just so frustrating because I know I should be able to just tune the background noise out, but every little beep or conversation just completely derails me.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly describes being easily derailed and losing their train of thought due to extraneous stimuli like beeping IV pumps, background conversations, and call lights.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back, did you experience similar difficulties with distractibility or staying focused when you were a child or in school?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. I mean, it’s funny you ask that because I was just talking to my mom about this recently. We were going through some old boxes at her house, and she actually found a bunch of my old report cards from elementary school. And it was honestly a little hard to read, because every single year, year after year, the teachers wrote the exact same thing in the comments section. They’d always say something like, "She’s so bright, she has so much potential," but then it was always followed by "but she’s just so careless." 

Which used to hurt my feelings so much, because I wasn't trying to be careless, you know? I really wanted to do a good job and be a good student. But I was just constantly, and I mean constantly, losing my worksheets. I'd shove them in my desk or my backpack and they'd just disappear into the void. Or I would actually do the homework—like, I would sit there and finish all the math problems—and then the next day I would just completely forget to turn it in. It would just sit in my folder while the teacher collected everyone else's, and I wouldn't even realize it until they handed them back graded. 

And my poor mom, she really tried everything to help me. She literally had to sit right next to me at the kitchen table every single night just to keep me on track. If she got up for even a second to stir a pot on the stove or answer the phone, I'd instantly be staring out the window or peeling the paper off my crayons or just daydreaming. She spent hours every week just redirecting me back to the paper in front of me. So, yeah, the distractibility is definitely not a new thing at all. It's just... I guess the stakes are so much higher now when I'm dealing with patient care than they were with third-grade spelling words, so I'm noticing it a lot more. But it's always been like this.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reports that her elementary school teachers consistently noted she was 'careless' in her work.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes needing her mother to sit next to her constantly to keep her on track with homework, indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states she was 'constantly losing my worksheets' which would disappear in her desk or backpack.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes that if left alone for a second, she would instantly become distracted by staring out the window, peeling crayons, or daydreaming.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient mentions she would completely forget to turn in her completed homework the next day.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from difficulties with focus, do you often feel physically restless, fidgety, or like you have an inner drive to keep moving?
turns.patient_response:
Um, no, not really. Actually, it's kind of the opposite, if I'm being completely honest. I don't have that... that physical energy or that need to move. Like, I know some people are always tapping their feet or pacing around, or they just can't sit still in a chair, but I've never really been like that. 

Even when I was a kid, going back to what I was saying about my mom, she never had to chase me around the house or tell me to stop climbing the furniture. I was always perfectly happy just sitting in one spot, usually just staring off into space or getting lost in my own head while she tried to get me to do my homework. 

And especially now, with my job? I mean, nursing is so physically demanding anyway. I'm on my feet for twelve hours a shift, running from room to room, pulling medications, helping patients to the bathroom, so by the time I actually get a second to sit down at the charting station, I am more than happy to just stay completely still. I don't feel that inner drive to keep moving at all. If anything, I feel like I have an inner drive to just lie down and not move a single muscle, just because my brain is working so hard all day trying to keep up with everything and filter out all that noise I mentioned. 

So, yeah, the fidgeting and the physical restlessness... that's really not something I struggle with. I mean, maybe I'll click a pen if it's right there in my hand, but I don't feel that overwhelming need to be in motion. It's really just the mental part that's the issue for me.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies fidgeting, stating they do not tap their feet or struggle with fidgeting.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient states they have never had trouble sitting still in a chair and were always perfectly happy sitting in one spot.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient denies physical restlessness and notes they never ran around or climbed on furniture inappropriately as a child.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly denies having an inner drive to keep moving or feeling like they are driven by a motor.
